title: The Playboy of the Western World
description: The greatest Irish comedy: a young man who claims to have killed his father becomes a hero in a Mayo shebeen.
plot_or_argument: Christy Mahon arrives at a public house in County Mayo claiming to have killed his father with a spade, and is celebrated by the villagers, the widow Quin and Pegeen Mike; when his father appears alive, the villagers turn on him, and Christy — having lost everything — goes out to meet his fate.
narrative_structure: Three acts in a single shebeen set, built on the repeated arrival.
principal_characters: Christy Mahon; Old Mahon; Pegeen Mike; Widow Quin; Michael James Flaherty; Shawn Keogh; Sara Tansey
literary_form: Play in three acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 26 January 1907)
historical_context: The west of Ireland, the peasant society of the Congested Districts, the oral story-telling tradition, and the nationalist politics of 1907, which made the play a riot on its first production.
literary_significance: The Playboy of the Western World is the greatest Irish play of the century and one of the great comedies in English: its language — Irish English made into poetry — is the finest invention of the revival, and its riot at the Abbey was the period's most famous theatrical scandal.

title: Riders to the Sea
description: The perfect one-act tragedy in English: a mother in the Aran Islands loses her last son to the sea.
plot_or_argument: Maurya has lost six sons and her husband to the sea; her last son Bartley insists on taking the horses to the mainland fair. While he is gone, the body of her drowned son Michael is brought in, and Bartley is killed when his horse throws him into the sea; the play ends with Maurya's great lament.
narrative_structure: Single act in a cottage kitchen, with the offstage sea as the antagonist.
principal_characters: Maurya; Bartley; Cathleen; Nora; the young priest; the women at the wake
literary_form: One-act tragedy (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 25 February 1904)
historical_context: The Aran Islands and the fishing economy of the Congested Districts; the keening tradition and the ritual lament of the Irish wake.
literary_significance: Riders to the Sea is the finest one-act tragedy in English: in twenty minutes it achieves the scale of Greek tragedy, its prose is the most musical in modern drama, and its lament is one of the great passages in Irish writing.

title: The Aran Islands
description: Synge's record of his visits to the Aran Islands: the finest English travel book about Ireland and the source of the language of his plays.
plot_or_argument: Synge describes four visits between 1898 and 1902: the cottages, the kelp-making, the fishing, the wakes, the story-tellers and the old men whose speech he transcribes almost phonetically, and his own slow acceptance by the islanders.
narrative_structure: Four parts corresponding to four visits, in diary and descriptive prose.
literary_form: Travel book (four parts)
historical_context: The Aran Islands and the Congested Districts Board, the last years of the Irish-speaking peasant culture, and the folklore collecting movement.
literary_significance: The Aran Islands is one of the great English travel books and the laboratory of Synge's art: the speech he recorded there became the language of the plays.

title: The Shadow of a Gunman
description: The first of O'Casey's Dublin plays: a poet is mistaken for an IRA gunman, with tragic consequences.
plot_or_argument: Donal Davoren, a poet sharing a tenement room with the pedlar Seumas Shields, is assumed by the neighbours to be an IRA man on the run. When a raid comes, the innocent Tommy Owens is killed and Davoren's illusions are exposed, in a play that turns from comedy to tragedy in its last minutes.
narrative_structure: Two acts in one tenement room, with the raid as the turning point.
principal_characters: Donal Davoren; Seumas Shields; Tommy Owens; Minnie Powell; Mr Maguire; Adolphus Grigson
literary_form: Play in two acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 1923)
historical_context: The Irish War of Independence (1919–21) and its aftermath, the Dublin tenements, and the cult of the gunman in nationalist Dublin.
literary_significance: The Shadow of a Gunman founded O'Casey's Dublin cycle and the modern Irish tragicomedy: it was the Abbey's first great success with a working-class play.

title: Juno and the Paycock
description: The great Dublin tenement tragedy: the Boyle family inherits a fortune that never arrives and is destroyed by the Civil War.
plot_or_argument: The Boyles — the boasting 'Captain' Boyle, his long-suffering wife Juno, their daughter Mary and their son Johnny — are told they have inherited a fortune. They furnish on credit; the inheritance collapses; Mary is pregnant and abandoned; and Johnny, who has betrayed a comrade, is shot and dragged away. The play ends with Juno taking her daughter away and Boyle left alone with his drunken friend Joxer.
narrative_structure: Three acts in a single tenement room, moving from comedy to tragedy.
principal_characters: Juno Boyle; 'Captain' Jack Boyle; Joxer Daly; Mary Boyle; Johnny Boyle; Maisie Madigan; Bentham
literary_form: Play in three acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 3 March 1924)
historical_context: The Irish Civil War (1922–23), the Dublin tenements, the irregular IRA and the official executions, and the class pretensions of the Dublin poor.
literary_significance: Juno and the Paycock is the greatest Irish tragedy of the century after Synge: its movement from farce to catastrophe, its musical working-class speech and Juno's final dignity make it a permanent play.

title: The Plough and the Stars
description: O'Casey's Easter Rising play: the tenement and the Rising seen from below, and the riot it caused.
plot_or_argument: In a Dublin tenement in 1915 and Easter week 1916, the inhabitants — the newly married Nora Clitheroe, her husband Jack, the ex-soldier, the union man and the prostitute Bessie Burgess — are caught up in the Rising. Jack is killed, Nora loses her baby and her mind, and Bessie is shot by a sniper while protecting Nora.
narrative_structure: Four acts: two in the tenement, one outside a pub, one in the tenement under fire.
principal_characters: Nora Clitheroe; Jack Clitheroe; Bessie Burgess; Fluther Good; Peter Flynn; the Covey; Rosie Redmond
literary_form: Play in four acts (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 8 February 1926)
historical_context: The Easter Rising of 1916, the Irish Citizen Army and the slum tenements of Dublin, and the nationalist sanctification of 1916 that the play attacked.
literary_significance: The Plough and the Stars is O'Casey's masterpiece: it refused the heroic version of 1916 and showed the Rising from the tenement, and the riots it provoked in 1926 drove O'Casey out of Ireland.

title: Dubliners
description: The founding book of the modern short story: fifteen stories of Dublin paralysis, and the epiphany as narrative technique.
plot_or_argument: The collection moves from childhood ('The Sisters', 'An Encounter', 'Araby') through adolescence ('Eveline', 'After the Race', 'Two Gallants', 'The Boarding House') and maturity ('A Little Cloud', 'Counterparts', 'Clay', 'A Painful Case') to public life, and ends with 'The Dead', in which Gabriel Conroy discovers his own emotional sterility at a Christmas party.
narrative_structure: Fifteen stories in five thematic groups, from childhood to public life, with 'The Dead' as coda.
principal_characters: Gabriel Conroy; Gretta Conroy; Eveline; Little Chandler; Farrington; Maria; Mrs Kearney
literary_form: Short-story collection (fifteen stories)
historical_context: Dublin at the turn of the century, the revival's claim to a national culture, the Catholic Church, the Parnell controversy and the paralysis of a colonial capital.
literary_significance: Dubliners invented the modern short-story sequence and the technique of the epiphany: its fifteen stories, written in what Joyce called a style of 'scrupulous meanness', gave the short story its modern discipline, and 'The Dead' is the greatest short story in English of the century.

title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
description: The novel of the artist's formation: Stephen Dedalus from infancy to exile, and the definitive novel of the aesthetic consciousness.
plot_or_argument: Stephen Dedalus grows up in Dublin: the Jesuit school of Clongowes, the family's decline, the sexual awakening, the retreat and the sermon on hell, the aesthetic revelation by the sea, and the university years in which he formulates his theory of art and decides to leave Ireland, 'to forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race'.
narrative_structure: Five chapters, each a stage of Stephen's life, with the prose developing alongside his consciousness.
principal_characters: Stephen Dedalus; Simon Dedalus; Mr Casey; Cranly; Emma Clery; Father Arnall
literary_form: Novel (serialized in The Egoist 1914–15)
historical_context: Dublin at the turn of the century, Irish Catholic education, the Parnell controversy, the revival and its nationalism, and the aesthetics of Aquinas and Aristotle.
literary_significance: A Portrait is the founding novel of the modern artist's self-making: its stream of consciousness, its development of style along with the mind it renders, and its theory of the epiphany made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of education.

title: Ulysses (Joyce, 1922)
description: The greatest novel of the century: a single Dublin day, every style at once, and the modern city rendered completely.
plot_or_argument: Leopold Bloom, a Jewish advertising canvasser, spends 16 June 1904 in Dublin: he makes breakfast, attends a funeral, works, lunches, is insulted by the Citizen in a pub, and returns home to his wife Molly, who has been unfaithful with Blazes Boylan. Stephen Dedalus wanders the same city and is rescued by Bloom in a brothel; at the end Bloom takes him home and Molly's soliloquy closes the book.
narrative_structure: Eighteen episodes, each with its own style and Homeric correspondence; three sections.
principal_characters: Leopold Bloom; Stephen Dedalus; Molly Bloom; Blazes Boylan; Buck Mulligan; the Citizen; Gerty MacDowell
literary_form: Novel (serialized in The Little Review 1918–20)
historical_context: Dublin on 16 June 1904, the Irish Literary Revival, nationalist and unionist politics, the Catholic Church, the Dublin Jewish community, and the Homeric parallel of the Odyssey.
literary_significance: Ulysses is the greatest novel of the twentieth century: it exhausted and renewed the form in eighteen episodes each in a different style, from interior monologue to newspaper headline to musical fugue to catechism to the unpunctuated female soliloquy. Its publication and the censorship battles that followed made it the central book of the period's literary freedom.
bibliographical_notes: Serialized in The Little Review from 1918 and stopped in 1921 by a New York obscenity prosecution; published by Shakespeare and Company in Paris on 2 February 1922; banned in Britain and the United States until the Woolsey decision of 1933.

title: Finnegans Wake
description: The most radical prose work in English: the dream of a Dublin publican, in a language made of every language.
plot_or_argument: Finnegan, a Dublin builder, is laid out for his wake; he becomes Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, the publican of Chapelizod, his wife Anna Livia Plurabelle, and their children Shem, Shaun and Issy. The seventeen chapters are the dream of Earwicker through a single night, in a language of portmanteau words, puns in dozens of languages, quotations and riddles, circling back to its own opening word.
narrative_structure: Four books of seventeen chapters, structured by Vico's cycles and the dream of a single night.
principal_characters: Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker (HCE); Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP); Shem the Penman; Shaun the Post; Issy
literary_form: Novel
historical_context: The history of Ireland, the Catholic Church, the Viking invasions, the fall of Parnell and the First World War, dissolved into the dream language of a Dublin family.
literary_significance: Finnegans Wake is the most radical work of prose in any language: it dissolved English into a dream language of portmanteau words, absorbed the whole history of the world into a Dublin night, and set the outer limit of the experimental novel.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Faber and Faber on 4 May 1939 after seventeen years of composition; sections appeared as Work in Progress from 1924.

title: Chamber Music
description: Joyce's early lyric sequence: Elizabethan-style songs of love and loss, written before the great prose.
plot_or_argument: The thirty-six poems follow a loose sequence of love, courtship, parting and loss in the manner of the Elizabethan songbook and the Irish lyric — the work of the young poet who would presently dismantle the lyric altogether.
narrative_structure: Thirty-six short lyrics in rhymed stanza, loosely sequenced.
literary_form: Poetry collection (thirty-six poems)
historical_context: The Dublin and Paris of the 1900s, the Irish lyric tradition and the fin-de-siècle aesthetic of the young Joyce.
literary_significance: Chamber Music is the foundation of Joyce's art and one of the purest bodies of lyric verse in modern English: several of its songs were set to music, and the collection shows the traditional discipline out of which the experimental prose came.

title: Prufrock and Other Observations
description: The first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady' and the urban lyric.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', 'Portrait of a Lady', 'Preludes', 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night', 'Aunt Helen' and 'The Boston Evening Transcript' — the poems of the modern city, the anti-heroic voice and the ironic quotation that founded English modernism.
narrative_structure: Twelve poems in free verse and irregular rhyme.
principal_characters: J. Alfred Prufrock; the lady of the portrait; the women who come and go
literary_form: Poetry collection (published by the Egoist Press)
historical_context: The Boston and London of the 1910s, the drawing rooms of the American aesthete, and the new urban consciousness of the modern city.
literary_significance: Prufrock and Other Observations is the first book of English modernism: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' made the anti-heroic voice the central instrument of modern poetry, and 'Preludes' and 'Rhapsody on a Windy Night' invented the modern urban lyric.

title: The Waste Land
description: The central poem of modernism: five sections of fragments, quotation and myth, and the modern world as a waste land.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with 'April is the cruellest month' and moves through the burial of the dead, the game of chess, the fire sermon, the death by water and 'What the Thunder Said': a collage of voices — Marie in the Hofgarten, the hyacinth girl, Madame Sosostris, Tiresias, the typist and the young man carbuncular, Phlebas the Phoenician — held together by the myth of the Fisher King and the search for rain.
narrative_structure: Five sections (The Burial of the Dead, A Game of Chess, The Fire Sermon, Death by Water, What the Thunder Said), 433 lines.
principal_characters: Tiresias; Madame Sosostris; Marie; the hyacinth girl; the typist; the young man carbuncular; Phlebas
literary_form: Long poem (five sections; first published in The Criterion, October 1922)
historical_context: Post-war London and Europe after 1918, the collapse of the old order, the Russian Revolution, and the anthropology of Frazer's Golden Bough and Weston's From Ritual to Romance, which Eliot cites in his notes.
literary_significance: The Waste Land is the central poem of modernism and the most influential poem of the century: its collage of quotation and mythic parallel created the modern long poem, its notes made allusion a public technique, and its vision of a civilisation in fragments defined the period's imagination. Pound's editing of the manuscript is the most famous act of modernist collaboration.
bibliographical_notes: Drafted 1921 and cut by Ezra Pound from a much longer manuscript; published in The Criterion (October 1922) and The Dial (November 1922), then by Boni and Liveright (New York, December 1922) with Eliot's notes. The manuscript was published in facsimile in 1971.

title: Four Quartets
description: Eliot's great religious poem: time, memory and the still point of the turning world.
plot_or_argument: The four poems — 'Burnt Norton' (1936), 'East Coker' (1940), 'The Dry Salvages' (1941), 'Little Gidding' (1942) — each in five movements, meditate on time, place, history and the possibility of incarnation. The sequence moves from a Gloucestershire rose garden to the village of Eliot's ancestors, to the Mississippi and the sea, to a bombed London street, and closes with 'the fire and the rose are one'.
narrative_structure: Four poems of five movements each, built on the analogy of the late Beethoven quartets.
literary_form: Poetry sequence (four poems, 1936–42; collected 1943)
historical_context: The Second World War, the London Blitz, Eliot's Anglo-Catholic faith, his visit to Little Gidding, and the air raids during which the last poem was written.
literary_significance: Four Quartets is the greatest English religious poem of the century and the summit of Eliot's achievement: it turned the modernist fragment into a sustained meditation on time, history and redemption and made the wartime London of the Blitz part of its structure.

title: Ash-Wednesday
description: Eliot's conversion poem: the turn from despair to faith, and the most penitential poem in modern English.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves from the speaker's refusal of hope and his ascent of the purgatorial stairs, through the vision of the lady and the yew trees, to the prayer for intercession that closes it.
narrative_structure: Six sections of varying length, with the refrain of the Lady and the yew trees.
literary_form: Poetry sequence (six sections)
historical_context: Eliot's baptism and confirmation in the Church of England in 1927, and his Anglo-Catholic faith of the late 1920s.
literary_significance: Ash-Wednesday is the great poem of Eliot's conversion and one of the central religious poems of the century: it is the bridge between The Waste Land and Four Quartets.

title: Murder in the Cathedral
description: Eliot's verse drama of the martyrdom of Thomas Becket: the great modern verse play in English.
plot_or_argument: The Chorus of the Women of Canterbury, the three priests and the four tempters prepare for the archbishop's return; Becket refuses the tempters' offers of power, pleasure, political action and martyrdom itself, preaches his Christmas sermon on the paradox of the martyr, and is murdered in the cathedral by the four knights, who then address the audience directly.
narrative_structure: Two parts, with a chorus, a sermon and the murder as the climax.
principal_characters: Thomas Becket; the Chorus of the Women of Canterbury; the three priests; the four tempters; the four knights
literary_form: Verse play (first performed in Canterbury Cathedral, 1935)
historical_context: The murder of Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170, and the political crisis of the 1930s, which made the play an allegory of the church against the totalitarian state.
literary_significance: Murder in the Cathedral is the great verse play of the period and the founding work of the modern revival of poetic drama: its chorus, ritual structure and analysis of the will made it a permanent work of the English stage.

title: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
description: Eliot's book of cat poems: light verse of the highest order, and the source of the musical Cats.
plot_or_argument: Fifteen poems introduce the cats of the tribe — Growltiger, the Rum Tum Tugger, Mr Mistoffelees, Macavity, Old Deuteronomy, Gus, Skimbleshanks and the rest — in nonsense verse of great technical accomplishment.
narrative_structure: Fifteen poems in varied stanza forms, with a mock-biological title.
principal_characters: Growltiger; Rum Tum Tugger; Mr Mistoffelees; Macavity; Old Deuteronomy; Gus; Skimbleshanks
literary_form: Poetry collection (children's verse)
historical_context: The Eliot household's cats, the letters Eliot wrote to his godchildren, and the English light verse tradition of Lear and Carroll.
literary_significance: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats is the finest book of children's verse of the period after the Alice books: its technical virtuosity in light verse is unmatched, and the poems became the basis of one of the longest-running musicals in history.

title: The Cantos
description: The modernist epic without an epic: a hundred and seventeen cantos of history, economics, myth and invective.
plot_or_argument: The Cantos begin with Odysseus's descent to the underworld and move through the Italian Renaissance, the Chinese ideogram, the American founding fathers, the troubadours, the Confucian order, the usury of the bankers, the Pisan prison camp and the wreck of the poet's own politics — assembling a history of civilisation out of quotation, translation and collage.
narrative_structure: One hundred and seventeen cantos in a collage of quotation, translation and juxtaposition.
principal_characters: Odysseus; Sigismundo Malatesta; John Adams; Confucius; the poet himself
literary_form: Long poem (A Draft of XVI Cantos, 1925; continued to 1970)
historical_context: Western and Chinese history as Pound understood it, the First World War, Italian fascism, the poet's imprisonment at Pisa in 1945, and the economic theories that led him to political catastrophe.
literary_significance: The Cantos are the great unfinished epic of modernism: they extended the method of The Waste Land to the scale of a civilisation, made the long poem a field rather than a narrative, and are inseparable from the political catastrophe of Pound's fascism — the period's central case of the poet's political failure.
bibliographical_notes: Published in instalments from A Draft of XVI Cantos (1925) to Drafts and Fragments (1969); the Pisan Cantos were written in the US Army detention camp at Pisa in 1945 and published in 1948.

title: Cathay
description: The most influential translation-poem of the century: versions of Chinese poetry made through the Fenollosa notebooks.
plot_or_argument: Pound's nineteen poems — 'The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter', 'The Jewel Stairs' Grievance', 'Lament of the Frontier Guard', 'South-Folk in Cold Country' — translate classical Chinese poetry through the notes of Ernest Fenollosa, creating a new English lyric of dramatic situation, precise image and withheld feeling.
narrative_structure: Nineteen poems translated from the Chinese, in free verse.
principal_characters: The river-merchant's wife; the frontier guard
literary_form: Poetry collection (translations from the Chinese)
historical_context: The Fenollosa notebooks, the Chinese poetry that had reached the West through the Imagist movement, and the First World War, during which the poems were written.
literary_significance: Cathay invented the modern translation-poem and gave English poetry a new idiom: its clean lines and dramatic situations made it the model for twentieth-century translation, and 'The River-Merchant's Wife' is one of the great English poems of the period.

title: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley
description: Pound's farewell to London and the finest short sequence of the period: the artist in a commercial civilisation.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows 'E.P.' — a poet modelled on Pound himself — through the aesthetic movements of the pre-war years, the War and the post-war literary market, and then 'Mauberley', the aesthete destroyed by the world he refuses; it closes with the vision of the poet as a failed fountain.
narrative_structure: Two parts: thirteen poems on 'E.P.' and five on Mauberley.
literary_form: Poetry sequence (two parts, thirteen and five poems)
historical_context: London in the 1910s, the First World War, the deaths of Gaudier-Brzeska and Henry James, and the commercial literary world Pound was leaving for Paris.
literary_significance: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley is the finest short sequence of the period and Pound's most perfectly achieved poem: its satire of the literary market, its elegy for the war dead and its self-portrait of the artist made it the model for the modernist sequence.
